title: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
hook: a child bends to an elder's feet, and a hand comes down on the child's head
carry: bow to what came before you

segments.voice: Yesterday, shanti, three times over. Your line was peace, peace, peace. When something rattled you, which of the three did it come from: the world, another person, or your own mind? Day five.

A grandmother comes through the front door with her bags. Before anyone says hello, a twelve-year-old crosses the room, bends down, and touches her feet. Her hand comes down and rests on the top of the child's head for a second. She says a few words under her breath. Then everybody goes back to arguing about dinner. The whole thing takes two seconds. If you grew up with it, your knees know it without thinking. If you didn't, it can look from the outside like bowing to a boss. Inside the gesture, something else is being said, and it goes in both directions. Today's word is the bow.
screen: `A CHILD BENDS TO THE FEET.` → `A HAND ON THE HEAD.` → `TWO SECONDS. TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Pranam. It's Sanskrit, built from pra, forward, and nam, to bend or bow. To bend forward: a respectful greeting. You met its cousin on day one. Namaste and pranam share that same bowing root. Touching the feet has its own name, charan sparsh. Charan, the feet. Sparsh, a touch. Here's one way it's explained. The head is the high point of a person, where the pride sits, and the opinions. The feet are the low point, and they've walked further down the road than yours have. So when the high point of you meets the low point of them, the gesture says something like: you've been where I'm going. Thank you. Now watch the other half. The elder doesn't just receive it. A hand comes down onto the head. That's a blessing, an ashirvad, given back. Respect is given. A blessing comes back. Nobody walks away smaller. An old law book, the Manusmriti, puts a promise on this habit. For the one who greets and serves elders, it says, four things grow: length of life, learning, good name and strength. Some read that as a promise, some as a description of what the habit does to a person. Either way, the gesture says one plain thing: nobody invents themselves. Somebody walked ahead, did hard things, and passed the road down. Pranam is a two-second way of saying so.
screen: `PRA + NAM — TO BEND FORWARD.` · `HIGH POINT MEETS LOW POINT.` · `RESPECT GIVEN, BLESSING BACK.` · `FOUR THINGS GROW.` · then, large: `YOU'VE BEEN WHERE I'M GOING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who came before you. A grandparent, a teacher, anyone who made your road easier, living or not. Let their face come clear. Then, with the bell, breathe in, and as you breathe out, bow to them in your mind. Or tip your head a little, for real. Stay bowed for one more breath, and picture the hand coming back, resting on your head. Whatever they'd have said, let them say it.
Pranam. To bend forward. A bow to the ones who walked first, and a blessing that comes back. Fifth word.
Your line: bow to what came before you. Today, thank one older person for one specific thing they did. A text is fine. That's day five.

screen: `DAY 5 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE AT EVERY DOORWAY.`

howItsDone: In Hindu families, children and younger adults greet parents, grandparents and teachers with pranam, often bending to touch their feet, and the elder answers with a hand on the head and a blessing.

original.note: Sanskrit: pra, forward, and nam, to bend. a bow of respect.

trapdoor: what you thought: bowing down to a boss.
what it means: thanks to someone further down the road, and a blessing that comes back.
what a scholar hears: pra + nam, to bend forward; Manusmriti 2.121 says life, learning, fame and strength grow for one who habitually greets and serves elders.

notes: Manusmriti 2.121 (abhivadana-shilasya nityam vriddhopasevinah, chatvari tasya vardhante ayur vidya yasho balam) paraphrased as 'length of life, learning, good name and strength'. Confirm the verse number; the same verse is also found in other texts. Keeper may prefer not to cite the Manusmriti on day 5 given its contested status; the teaching stands without it.
'One way it's explained' (head as the high point, feet as having walked the road) is a popular explanation, not a scriptural one; confirm.
Charan sparsh and ashirvad given in common Hindi spelling; confirm transliteration.

Cut from manuscript day 5 under the claims rule: 'walked for five thousand years', 'no book explains as well', 'Most people say the third', and the specific gesture of crossed hands (Manusmriti 2.72) to keep it simple.
Hook uses a twelve-year-old in the scene; the age is part of the picture, not a claim.

Audit pass: 'respect goes down, blessing comes up' had the directions backwards (the blessing comes down onto the head); now 'respect is given, a blessing comes back' in the teach, screen head, myth reveal and day 6 review screen.

Editor pass: practice reshaped so it no longer repeats the 'three breaths with the bell, on the first / second / third' template used on days 3, 4 and 6; same steps (bring someone to mind, bow, the hand coming back). Checked Manusmriti 2.121's four things (life, learning, fame, strength) against the paraphrase; no other changes.

Editor review 2: the 'promise or description, either way the point is the same' line was filler, and 'you didn't invent yourself' told the listener about themselves; now attributed to readers and to the gesture.
